target_customer: Governments, weather agencies and shipping companies that need frequent ocean surface wind and weather data
problem: Weather forecasts rely on aging government satellites and sparse sensors, so ocean winds are observed infrequently. Care Weather aims to give hourly, high accuracy ocean surface observations from cheap radar satellites.
business_model: Data sales to government and maritime customers from its own satellite constellation, plus government grants
product_category: Small radar satellites (scatterometer) for ocean surface winds and weather data

founders.name: Patrick Walton
education: Brigham Young University, M.S. and B.S. in electrical and mechanical engineering
founders.background_notes: YC page says he started BYU's rocketry club and led a 20-person team funded by $1M from NASA to launch BYU's first two satellites; company description calls him a NASA Earth science fellow.

founders.name: Alex Laraway
education: Brigham Young University, B.S. in manufacturing
founders.background_notes: YC page says he flew rockets to Mach 4 and built several satellites now in orbit. Surname appears only on the YC page; the launch post gives only first names.

competitors.name: Spire Global
competitors.what: Commercial nanosatellite constellation selling weather and maritime data including radio occultation
competitors.traction_then: listed among dominant commercial weather data providers by a market overview; undated

competitors.name: Government weather satellites (NOAA, JTWC sources)
competitors.what: Aging government satellites, weather stations, balloons and drones cited by the YC launch post as the incumbent data sources

technical_complexity.rationale: A flat-panel radar satellite small enough for a cubesat-class launch required novel hardware and radar design; the team says it built and launched what it called the smallest radar satellite ever.

defensibility.rationale: Deep radar and satellite hardware know-how and operating spacecraft in orbit are hard to copy, but commercial weather data buyers had other suppliers.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Tomorrow.io launched its own radar satellite in 2023 per a search summary, so peers moved into the space; no acquisition of Care Weather found.

market_need_then: Launch post cites aging government satellites and non scalable stations as the data source, and the company reported letters of intent from the Air Force, National Weather Service and shippers (stated as $35M on the YC profile and $50M in the launch post; unverified).

identity.mascot_or_character: Satellites carry bird names, with the product line called Veery (a songbird)
identity.voice_and_tone: Mission oriented, about adapting to extreme weather

brand_strength.rationale: No press about the brand itself found; the descriptive company name and bird named satellites are the only identity signals in sources.

outcome_analysis: Care Weather is still operating and has flown multiple Veery satellites since its 2021 pre-seed and a 2023 NSF grant. Its founders have deep satellite engineering backgrounds, which fits a hardware heavy problem. Public funding is thin and only grant and pre-seed money is found, so whether it can raise a larger round is not yet shown.
notes: Funding totals are only from aggregators (CB Insights about $1.27M, others differ); the pre-seed investor list comes from Bounce Watch and Extruct summaries, amount unknown. The NSF grant amount is from CB Insights only. Competitor list is thin: Spire is a rival listed on an alternatives page, undated, so as-of-founding traction is not sourced. Tomorrow.io radar satellite launched after founding and is not listed as a competitor.
